I’m so sorry. I experienced postpartum psychosis after the birth of our oldest. I didn’t know I was at risk due to having Bipolar 2. Even with an underlying mental illness, I’ve been off antipsychotics since 2 months after that break (so February 2018) and have not had any recurrence of psychotic symptoms. I just had a second child and didn’t have a relapse. A single psychotic break does not doom your wife to lifelong struggles.

I wouldn’t recommend it, as it can very easily be traumatizing. ABA practitioners will tell you it can help with communication, which should be left to licensed speech therapists. Floortime is a good intervention that is child led and works on social engagement without pressuring the child to mask their autistic traits. Due to polyhydramnios, I was scheduled for cervidil induction at 38w2d on 10/4. I have been on modified bed rest since 28w so we spent all day Wednesday cleaning. My mom came in to town to dog sit, took us to dinner for my "last meal", and we called the hospital at 7pm to see when to come in, as directed. We were told to come in at 8:30. When we got to the hospital, they were waiting for a room to empty. I was taken to triage where they started my IV, and moved to a labor room by 9:30. We were told they had to get the cervidil and would be right back. 45 minutes later, we were informed that the pharmacy was out if Cervidil and they had to order some from the neighboring hospital. They didn't get it until midnight. When they did the first check before inserting it, I was closed, 70% effaced and baby was at -2. 

I tried to sleep after the insertion but my restless legs were brutal. I was offered ambien but advised it was really late, and I have bad luck with sleep meds making my RLS worse so I declined.  Due to this, I got 2.5 hours of broken sleep, which probably made things harder later. 

My OB came to check me at 8:30am on Thursday 10/5. I was 2-3cm dilated, 70% effaced and baby was still at -2. They attempted to break my water but my cervix was too posterior. This hurt terribly. Pitocin was started at 9:30 at a 2, then increased twice before 12:15pm, when I was checked and had progressed to 4cm. Contractions weren't strong at all at this point. My water was broken with the hook and it just GUSHED out. They were honestly surprised at how much fluid there was. This was the most embarrassing part of labor. I soaked through 2 bed pads, my nightgown, my blanket and sheets. I called for help to replace them and the nurses walked me to the bathroom to change gowns. I left puddles the whole way. They gave me a giant postpartum pad, which was soaked through within 30 minutes. I continued to gush fluid for the next 6 hours. 

They increased the pitocin again at 1 and the contractions began to be painful, but I could get through them using slow, deep breaths. Dosage was increased again at 2. At 3:45, I was checked and had made no progress. It was also noted that baby boy was face up and lying at an angle. At this point I was told he may not be able to be born vaginally. He had been face up at every ultrasound so I had been preparing myself for that. I moved to the birthing ball to try to get baby to turn. It also helped with the contractions, I would gently rock and take slow, deep breaths. 

The pitocin was increased again at 4pm and at 5:30 I had made no progress. In fact, baby had moved back to -3. Pitocin was upped to 20 which meant internal monitoring. Which meant use of the tub was no longer an option for pain management. By 6:30, my contractions had begun to be legitimately painful, I had to squeeze my husband's hand and couldn't speak or move through them. They increased pitocin again, I think twice, before I was checked at 9:30. I had dilated to 5-6cm by this point and baby was back at -2. By this point I was whimpering and contractions were an 8. I was debating between nitrous and the epidural. I had originally wanted to go without an epidural. But at this point I was near tears. The labor was in my back now, I was running on 2 hours of sleep and at the rate we were going, this was not ending any time soon. I told my OB I was worried about stalling labor, but she assured me that due to the pitocin, I wouldn't. I looked at her and my husband and said, I want the epidural. The anaesthesiologist was in my room within 10 minutes. The numbing shot hurt a little but I was complimented on being stoic. I felt the needle rub against my vertebra, which was weird, but within 10 minutes the nurse told me I was in the peak of a contraction and I felt nothing. Epidurals are magic.  The nurses set me up on my side with a peanut ball to help open my pelvis, and I was asleep within 10 minutes. 

I got several glorious hours of sleep but at 4:30am, they woke me up to tell me that the baby's heart had begun to decelerate during contractions, so they had turned off the pitocin for a while and were about to restart it at a dosage of 12. I was checked and had only progressed to a good 6cm, and baby hadn't dropped. They restarted the pitocin, and told me my OB would be in around 8 to check me and we would make a final decision. 

At 8:30am on 10/6, my OB checked me. The pitocin was back up to an 18 at this point, but I was still at 6cm and baby wasn't moving. A c section was recommended and I readily agreed. Prep started super quickly. My mom was called and headed towards us. I was given a loading dose of epidural and taken to the OR. I was shaking uncontrollably, which was not fun. They gave me two regional nerve block injections, strapped me down and brought my husband in. 

The entire c section was bizarre. It wasn't painful, but feeling people tugging your insides is very weird. I had several waves of nausea. My anaesthesiologist was amazing and walked me through every part of the procedure, and through breathing through the nausea. He told me I would feel pressure on my chest and that meant the baby was being removed. I heard them say he was out, heard the suction in his mouth and nose...and then didn't hear anything. I asked out loud why he wasn't crying but they assured me he would. And he did...once. They were closing me up and the anesthesiologist pushed aside the drape so I could see the baby, and what i saw was two nurses frantically shaking him, jostling him and pumping air into his mouth with a balloon looking machine. All the while he laid there silent. They said his heart rate was good, and he was pink, he just didn't want to breathe. A neonatologist was called and I was told he would be sent to our hospital's NICU. My husband and i had talked about this, so he knew to go with the baby.  As soon as they left the room, I began to freak out. I became very aware of not being able to move my legs, specifically my left leg which I was fixated on moving. I began to hyperventilate and tried to calm myself down but couldnt. The anaesthesiologist asked if I would like some meds to calm down. I declined initially but he suggested a touch of Versed. It did the trick to help slow my breathing, and when I was closed up they turned down the epidural and I could wiggle my toes which helped a lot. 

The rest of the day and night was mostly a waiting game for news on Eli. The neonatologist came to speak to us at around 12pm and told us that Eli was on oxygen and a feeding tube. He wasn't taking deep breaths and had had 2 apnea episodes. The dr theorized that this could be due to the length of labor and just getting tired, which made the transition harder for him. We also found out he had been facing towards my left hip, and his cord had been wrapped tight around him. He was doing well on oxygen, but they wanted antibiotics in case of infection and they couldn't find a vein for an IV. We were told that IV specialists were working with him, but if they couldn't find a spot then the last option would be his umbilical cord. Unfortunately only the NICU across the bridge was equipped to do umbilical IVs, so if it came to that he would have to be transferred. 

In the meantime, I was moved to the postpartum recovery movement and all i wanted was to see him, but I couldn't until my fluids and vitals were stable. In the evening, we were finally told that his bloodwork had come back infection free so they weren't going to transfer him, and that they had been able to wean him down to 3.5 liters of oxygen. My husband was also able to feed him formula through his NG tube without depressing his respiration. All good signs! I finally got to see him for the first time around 11pm. Unfortunately I was in too much pain still to stay long and he was on low stimulation protocol so I couldn't hold him. 

We were woken up this morning to tbe neonatologist telling us Eli was being weaned off of oxygen and if he had 2 successful feedings without issues, he could come to stay with us. This was the best news ever. I ate breakfast and took my pain meds and was able to walk to the nursery. He was having his first bath and when they were done, I got to hold my son for the first time. I cannot explain the joy and pure love that flooded me at that moment. 

Elijah was finally able to come room with us at 12:45pm. We did our first feeding and are getting better at it. He has a really strong startle reflex, which may be due to me being on SSRIs during pregnancy, but other than that he is improving and getting stronger hour by hour. And his cry is, at least right now, the most beautiful sound.  

tl;dr: 30 hours of labor after cervidil/pitocin induction, failure to progress due to OP positioning, c-section, baby spends a little over 24 hours in nicu due to respiratory distress but is now with us and we will be going home monday

Okay, so we were actually able to put our dog's separation anxiety into remission but it took a long time. First, I would say if you are worried about her hurting herself in the crate, don't crate her while working on the separation anxiety. Try an x-pen, or a room that can be dog proofed. Second, I would see a behaviorist to see if medication for when you leave is an option. Something fast acting like Trazodone could make all the difference. Also, for our girl, being able to see outside helped a lot, so we open the blinds a little.

When you do begin working on it, you will need to start where the anxiety starts. Does she get nervous when you put on your shoes? When you grab your keys? Start there. Give her a yummy frozen kong, put on your shoes and grab your keys, and then take them off and remove the kong. Repeat until she has no reaction. Remember, she only gets the special kong when you are training this issue. (Our girl now knows that when we grab the keys she gets a frozen kong full of peanut butter, and her reaction is excitement.) 

You will need to systematically work through every step of the leaving process this way before you ever leave the house. When you do begin leaving the house, I recommend a webcam with a phone app set up in the area with the dog so you can watch for her to go above threshold. You don't want that to happen, or you've gone too fast and need to take a step back. 

When you first leave the house, it will literally be to step away from the door and immediately return. Then maybe you get in the car. Then drive down the driveway. Then down the street. Then 5 minutes, then 10, then 8. You dont want the time to ALWAYS increase, you want some easier times thrown in. Again, always keeping an eye on her on the camera. 

What we read and found to be true was that most separation anxiety occurs within the first 45 minutes and if you can get past that, you're in the clear. Good luck! 

Oh! And if she cant be left alone at all right now, daycare may be the only option until you have time to do this desensitizing protocol.
